1:
That a second feeding so like the first should occur at all is met head on. Robertson reports that the repetition disturbs modern critics who cannot imagine Jesus performing another miracle so similar to the earlier one, and answers them from the text: both evangelists give both miracles, both distinguish the two different words for baskets, and both have Jesus afterwards refer to the two incidents keeping the same distinction — so that it is easier to conceive he wrought two such miracles than to hold that the evangelists made a jumble of the whole business. Clarke contributes a textual variant that leans the same way, preferring the reading that makes this again a great multitude rather than a very great one, on the authority of many manuscripts and versions and with Griesbach's approval, and noting that such a multitude had been gathered once before. Theophylact answers the question of motive rather than history: the Lord did not always work miracles about feeding, lest men should follow him for the sake of food, and he would not have worked this one had he not seen the multitude in danger.

The compassion is read for what it proves about the person. Bede makes the verse a test case in doctrine, arguing that one and the same Redeemer is seen here in a distinct operation of Divinity and of Manhood, and that the error of Eutyches, who would lay down a single operation in Christ, is to be cast far out of the Christian pale — for who does not see that the pity for the multitude is the feeling and sympathy of humanity, while the satisfying of four thousand with seven loaves is a work of Divine virtue? Gregory turns the same clause into a rule for preachers, that men must find in what is preached the word of consolation, lest hungering for want of the food of truth they sink under the toil of this life. Ambrose presses it on the hearer instead: the good Lord requires diligence and gives strength, and will not dismiss men fasting either in the course of this life or before they reach the fountainhead of life; he is the Dispenser of all things, but whoever refuses to stretch forth his hand to receive cannot find fault with him who pities and divides.
3:
Who the crowd were, and what following cost them, is Henry's subject. He notes that Jesus was greatly followed in spite of the arts of the scribes and Pharisees, the common people having more honesty and therefore more true wisdom than their leaders; that these were generally of the meaner sort, with whom Christ was familiar because he had made himself of no reputation; and that they underwent real hardship, being three days with him and having nothing to eat. From that he draws two remarks, that no Pharisee should say Christ's disciples do not fast, and that true zeal makes nothing of hardships in the way of duty, since those who have a full feast for their souls may be content with slender provision for their bodies — recalling an old saying among the Puritans that bread and the gospel are good fare. He adds the contrast the scene turns on, that whom the proud Pharisees looked upon with disdain the humble Jesus looked upon with pity. Gill and Clarke measure the danger in the clause about sending them away fasting. Gill notes that the Greek has the singular, to their own house or home, but that all the Oriental versions render it in the plural, and that from this it seems they were now fasting and had at least had no food all that day, whatever they might have had the day before, which is not certain; Clarke adds that divers of them could not possibly reach their respective homes without perishing, unless they got food.

The disciples' question is the chapter's first difficulty, and nobody excuses it on the facts. Gill states it plainly, that they had forgotten the late feeding of five thousand though they now had a smaller number and more provisions. Robertson says they feel as helpless as before and do not rise to faith in the unlimited power of Jesus after all they have seen. Theophylact agrees that they neither understood nor believed in his virtue notwithstanding former miracles, but makes the response the lesson: the Lord does not blame them, teaching us not to be grievously angry with ignorant men but to bear with their ignorance. Ellicott and Robertson both stop on small words, Ellicott noting that the clause about coming from afar is spoken by our Lord and stands in the perfect tense, and that the term for the desert place is abstract rather than concrete and suggests loneliness; Robertson notes that the detail of their coming from far is in Mark alone.
5:
Why the question about the loaves was asked at all is answered as it was in the earlier feeding. Remigius says ignorance was not the reason, but that from their answering seven the miracle might be noised abroad and become better known in proportion to the smallness of the number. He also marks the one visible difference from the former occasion, that there the people lay on grass and here on the ground, and draws from the giving of thanks an example, that for all gifts conferred from heaven we should return thanks. Bede turns the same difference into doctrine: the earlier feeding signified the letter of the Old Testament full of spiritual grace, this one the truth and grace of the New, and where the law bids us keep under the desires of the flesh the New Testament bids us leave even the earth itself and our temporal goods. Ellicott corrects the posture entirely, noting that the Greek implies the usual Eastern reclining rather than our sitting, and Robertson watches the tenses, a single act of breaking followed by an imperfect that keeps the giving going.

The distribution is read as a picture of ministry. Remigius observes that our Lord did not give the bread to the people but to his disciples, and the disciples to the people, and that he blessed the fish as well and ordered them set before the crowd. Bede reads the same order allegorically, that the breaking of the bread means the opening of mysteries, the giving of thanks shows how great a joy he feels in the salvation of the human race, and the handing of the loaves to the disciples signifies that he assigns the spiritual gifts of knowledge to the Apostles so that the food of life should be distributed by their ministry. Cyril of Jerusalem reads the gesture eucharistically instead, setting beside it the Apostle's account of the night of the betrayal, and asking who shall dare doubt after the words over the bread and the cup. Wesley draws the plainest doctrine of all, that the miracle was intended to demonstrate that Christ is the true bread which comes down from heaven, since he who was almighty to create bread without means to support natural life could not want power to do the same for spiritual life.
7:
The numbers are then allegorised three different ways, and the schemes do not agree. Theophylact takes the three days for the baptized, since baptism is called illumination; the seven loaves for spiritual discourses, seven being the number that points to the Holy Ghost who perfects all things, as our life is perfected in seven days; and the four thousand for men perfect in the four virtues, who being more advanced ate more and therefore left fewer fragments than the earlier multitude. Pseudo-Jerome makes the seven loaves the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the seven baskets the seven Churches, and reads the four thousand as the year of the new dispensation with its four seasons; the small fishes he takes for the books of the New Testament, since the risen Lord asked for a piece of broiled fish, or else for the saints themselves, snatched from the troubled waves of this world. Bede keeps to his contrast between the Old Testament and the New, and reads the distance the people travelled morally, that those who return to repentance after crimes of the flesh come to the Lord from afar, in proportion as a man has wandered farther in evil working, and that the believing Gentiles came from afar while the Jews came from near, having been taught by the letter of the law and the prophets.

What was left over draws the last remarks, and two of them are about a word. Robertson insists the term means an overplus or abundance, the remains of broken pieces not used, and not merely scraps or crumbs; Ellicott renders it simply as fragments. Theophylact notices who gathered them, that the multitude did not carry off the remains but the disciples took them up, and makes it a lesson that we should be content with what is sufficient and look for nothing beyond; he adds that Christ sends no one away fasting, since he wishes all to be nourished by his grace. Gill marks what is amazing in the account and what is merely surprising: that the food could be divided so far that every one had a piece is surprising, but that all should be satisfied to the full is the astonishing thing. Robertson notes one small oddity of arrangement, that Mark mentions the fishes last, as though they were served after the food.
10:
The place he crosses to is named differently in the two Gospels, and the witnesses are content to leave it unsettled. Augustine says we cannot doubt it is the same place under another name, and notes that several manuscripts even of Mark have only the other form. Ellicott takes the divergence as evidence of something else, that Mark's use of a name mentioned by no other writer is an instance of his independence. Robertson agrees both names are unknown elsewhere while placing them in the same region of Galilee on the western side of the lake, and notices that Mark alone says the disciples were with him. Theophylact supplies the motive for the crossing rather than the geography, that after the miracle of the loaves he retires at once lest the multitudes take him to make him a king. Gill places the departure immediately after the dismissal of the crowd, Jesus taking ship as soon as he had sent them away, since he was then either at the sea of Galilee or upon its shore.

What the Pharisees were asking for is described with some precision. Theophylact takes them to want the sun and moon made to stand still, hail brought down, the atmosphere changed, because they supposed he could work no miracle from heaven and could do signs on earth only by Beelzebub. Bede reads the demand as an appeal to precedent, that he who had twice fed thousands with a few loaves should now, after the example of Moses, refresh the whole nation with manna sent down from heaven. Henry describes the manner rather than the content, that they came forth on purpose to question with him, not to propose questions that they might learn but to cross question him that they might ensnare; and he observes that a sign from heaven had already been given at the baptism, in the descent of the dove and the voice, which they might have seen had they attended. Robertson adds that the Pharisees have now been joined by the Sadducees for the first time, and that they began a dispute rather than an inquiry and kept it up.

Why no sign was given at all is answered by the fathers from the calendar of providence. Theophylact says the time of signs from heaven had not arrived, that being the time of the second Advent when the powers of heaven shall be shaken and the moon not give her light, whereas in the first Advent all things are full of mercy. Bede answers by the audience rather than the hour: a sign from heaven was not to be given to a generation that tempted the Lord, but to a generation seeking him he shows one, when in the sight of the Apostles he ascended into heaven. Henry doubts that a sign would have helped in any case, since obstinate unbelief will have something to say however unreasonable, and holds that if they will not be convinced they shall not.
12:
The groan is examined more closely than anything else in the paragraph. Robertson notes the verb is the only instance of its compound in the New Testament, the preposition intensifying it, and quotes the judgement that the sigh seemed to come from the bottom of his heart and that the Lord's human spirit was stirred to its depths. Gill locates the cause in the hardness of their hearts, the malignity of their minds and the insincerity of their intentions, since they had no view to come at truth by the enquiry. Bede sets the groan against the thanksgiving of the previous scene and makes the pair a portrait of one nature: bearing about with him the feelings of human nature, as he rejoices over the salvation of men so he grieves over their errors. Calvin presses the same point against an imagined objector, that the words are added emphatically to show the groan proceeded from the deepest affection of his heart, so that no sophist might allege that Christ resorted to outward attitudes to express a grief he did not inwardly feel. Henry generalises it, that the infidelity of those who have long enjoyed the means of conviction is a great grief to the Lord Jesus, since it troubles him that sinners should stand in their own light and put a bar in their own door.

The form of the refusal is a Hebrew idiom, and two witnesses centuries apart identify it the same way. Bede reads the clause as an oath with its conclusion left unspoken, comparing the Psalm in which God swears once by his holiness if I shall fail David, meaning that he will not fail him; so here the sense is that no sign shall be given. Robertson reaches the identical conclusion by grammar, calling it technically a conditional clause with the conclusion unexpressed, an aposiopesis imitating the Hebrew, and the only instance of the construction in the New Testament outside quotations. Whether the refusal was absolute is a separate question. Augustine insists the two accounts do not conflict, since Mark's blank refusal must be understood of such a sign as they asked, that is one from heaven, Mark having simply omitted what the other evangelist reports about the prophet; Barnes says the same, that a sign was promised but not the one demanded and not because they demanded it; Ellicott only notes the omission; Robertson quotes the contrary judgement that the mention of that prophet was itself an absolute refusal of signs in their sense.

Whether it was worth staying to argue is answered by the departure that follows. Robertson notes drily that the rabbis were splitting hairs over the miracles as having a possible natural explanation, as some critics do today, and that when he did rise on the third day the council refused to be convinced. Lightfoot meets the demand with a story rather than a comment, and the story cuts against the questioners: he relays the rabbinic account of a teacher who, unable to win assent for his tradition, called successively on a tree, on a river and on the walls of the school to bear him witness, and got each sign in turn — the tree rooted up and moved, the waters turned backward, the walls bowing as if to fall — and was answered each time that a proof is not to be fetched from such things, until at last a voice from heaven itself was heard on his side. Theophylact draws the practical rule from the leaving, that where there is hope of correction it is right to remain but where the evil is incorrigible we should go away; and Gill says the same of it, that these were men with whom it was not worth while to discourse.
14:
That the disciples had no bread just after gathering seven baskets is an oddity two fathers notice and value oppositely. Bede raises it as a question — how could they have none, when they had filled seven baskets before embarking? — and answers that Scripture says they forgot to take them, which he treats as a credit to them, a proof how little care they had for the flesh, since in their eagerness to follow the Lord even the necessity of refreshing their bodies had escaped their minds. Theophylact makes the same forgetfulness a discipline rather than a virtue, holding that by a special providence they forgot, so that they might be blamed by Christ and thereby become better and arrive at a knowledge of his power. Ellicott and Robertson keep to the detail itself: Ellicott reads the verse as continuous with what precedes rather than as the opening of a new section and notes the single loaf as another item peculiar to Mark; Robertson adds the arithmetic that makes it vivid, one loaf for thirteen hungry men.

Who the second party is differs between the Gospels, and every witness has a way of squaring it. Barnes takes it that Christ probably cautioned them against all three, since the Pharisees sought his life and were corrupt in doctrine and practice, the Sadducees denied essential doctrines, and the Herodians held it lawful for the Jews to acknowledge a foreign prince, so that one evangelist recorded the warning against two parties and the other supplied the third; thus, he concludes, the evangelists speak the same thing. Pseudo-Chrysostom reaches the same result by counting: all three accounts name the Pharisees as the chief party, while two of them each mention one of the secondary sects, so that Mark's addition of Herod is a supplement to the other narrative. Ellicott infers from the phrase that others besides Pharisees must have been among the questioners a few verses earlier. Wesley describes the pair as two opposite extremes, and Robertson divides them by kind, warning against bad politics on the one hand and bad theology on the other.

What the leaven itself stands for is given in three different registers. Theophylact reads it as hurtful and corrupt doctrine full of the old malice, and identifies the Herodians as teachers who said that Herod was the Christ. Bede supplies a catalogue for each: the leaven of the Pharisees is the making of the decrees of the divine law inferior to the traditions of men, preaching the law in word while attacking it in deed, tempting the Lord and disbelieving his doctrine; the leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, rash swearing, a pretence of religion and hatred of Christ and his forerunner. He then completes the figure, that if the leaven means perverse traditions, the food with which the people of God was nourished means the true doctrine. Robertson and Ellicott both note that the warning was repeated: the tense is imperfect, so that the charge was given more than once, which Robertson takes as showing how badly it was needed, the disciples having come out of a Pharisaic atmosphere and met it again at the place they had just left.
17:
The rebuke is a string of questions, and Mark keeps more of them than the parallel. Robertson counts six keen questions here against four in the other Gospel that run some of them together, and sets out what each touches — the intellect, the heart in a hardened state, the eyes, the ears, and the memory of both feedings, sharply distinguished even to the two different words for baskets. Ellicott notes that the question about the hardened heart is peculiar to Mark, as are the first two of the next verse, and that the expression of indignant astonishment is characteristically more vivid and emphatic in his report. Gill takes the eyes and ears both ways, of the body and of the understanding, since they had seen the miracles with bodily eyes and taken little notice, while the eyes of their understanding, though enlightened by Christ, still saw things very darkly.

How severe the diagnosis is meant to be is where the witnesses part, and Wesley guards it carefully. He grants that our Lord here affirms of all the apostles, the question being equivalent to an affirmation, that their hearts were hardened and that having eyes they saw not, in the very same expressions used elsewhere of outsiders; and then he draws the line, that it is certain they were not judicially hardened, so that all these strong expressions need not import anything more than a present want of spiritual understanding. Robertson lets the severity stand and quotes two harsher judgements, that Jesus administers a sharp rebuke for their preoccupation with mere temporalities as if there were nothing higher to be thought of, and that for the time the Twelve are wayside hearers with hearts like a beaten path, into which the higher truths cannot sink so as to germinate. Gill sits between them, allowing enlightenment and dimness together.

What the questions were for is answered by their own content. The two feedings are recalled in order, and the disciples prove able to give the numbers of baskets in each case, twelve and seven, which is precisely the point: the memory was intact and the inference was not made. Robertson reads the final question as the measure of the failure, that after all this rebuke and explanation they still did not understand, and remarks that the greatest of all teachers had the greatest of all classes and struck a snag here; he notes from the parallel that they did understand in the end, that the warning was not about loaves of bread but about the teaching of the Pharisees, and observes that they had once claimed to understand the parables, but that was a long time ago, and that the teacher must have patience if his pupils are to understand. Gill marks the same sequence more plainly, that since they remembered the miracles and their circumstances so well, the question that follows is the one they could not answer.
22:
The town is identified and the miracle marked as unique to this Gospel. Ellicott says the cure is recorded by Mark only, and judges from the places named before and after that this is the Bethsaida on the north-eastern shore; Robertson puts it on the eastern side not far from the feeding of the five thousand, notices the dramatic present tenses by which they come and they bring, and adds that the place had been a village until Philip enlarged it into a town, though the narrative still calls it one. Gill supplies the local colour, a fishing town and the city of Andrew and Peter and Philip, and dismisses a variant reading that gives another name altogether.

Why he took the man out of the town is answered five ways. Henry argues from what was not done: had privacy alone been wanted, a house or an inner chamber would have served, so the leading out was meant to upbraid Bethsaida with the mighty works done there in vain, telling her in effect that she was unworthy to have more done within her walls; though he also allows a practical motive, that the open fields gave a larger prospect on which to try the recovered sight. Clarke and Wesley take the same view of the reproach, Clarke adding that when a people do not improve the light they receive their candlestick is removed. Theophylact locates the fault in the bystanders instead, that the faith of those who brought the man was not true faith, so that he was led away lest he take hurt in his soul from them. Barnes proposes the opposite kind of reason, that Christ wished to avoid a multitude and the designs of the Pharisees, showing that while he did good he desired to do it in a way that avoided the appearance of evil. Robertson declines to choose, observing only that Jesus keeps the utmost secrecy here as in the other cure Mark alone records, for reasons not given, and suggesting that this was the season of retirement from Galilee.

The spittle draws four incompatible explanations. Barnes denies any natural efficacy and makes it a sign: the eyes were probably gummed shut, and to wet them was a natural expression of removing the obstruction, but the power was not in the spittle, it only attended the application. Clarke goes further in the same direction and turns it into a rule about miracles: it is likely the spittle was used merely to separate the eyelids, since that required no miracle and natural means were therefore employed, whereas the restoring of sight did; and he generalises that false miracles are wrought without reason or necessity and are detected by it, while true miracles never effect by power what could be done by natural means. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads both gestures as symbols, the hand standing for working and the spittle for the word proceeding out of the mouth, so that the effects of the Divine word added to action might be shown. Bede takes the spittle, as proceeding from the Head, to point out the grace of the Holy Ghost, and the taking of the hand as a strengthening for the practice of good works. Ellicott adds the literary observation, that this and the cure of the deaf man are the only instances of the gesture in the first three Gospels, and that it is one of the links connecting Mark with the fourth.
24:
Why the cure came by stages is the chapter's best question, and it gets five answers and one refusal. Theophylact says the man did not see perfectly at once because he had not perfect faith, since healing is bestowed in proportion to faith; Pseudo-Chrysostom says the same of the weak faith both of the man and of those who brought him, and notes that the question whether he could see anything was put to no one else Christ healed. Bede makes it a demonstration rather than a limitation, that though by one word he could have cured the man wholly and at once, he cures by degrees to show the greatness of human blindness, which can hardly and only step by step be restored to light. Barnes makes it pedagogy: a partial restoration was evidence that Christ could restore wholly, and so drew the man to exercise faith anew. Calvin refuses every reason drawn from the patient and locates it entirely in the physician, holding that Christ proceeded so in order to prove that he had full liberty as to his method and was not restricted to a fixed rule, so that the grace which had before been poured out suddenly on others flowed by drops, as it were, on this man. Robertson simply records that this is the single case of a gradual cure among the healings and that the reason for the method is not given.

The half-sight itself is described with unusual care. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts give two different words for two forms of perception, so that the man beholds men but sees them walking as trees, and remarks that the naturalness of this first impression of a restored sense strikes every reader. Calvin presses the logic of the sentence: the man acknowledges that his sight is not yet clear enough to distinguish, and speaks only by conjecture, inferring from the motion that those he perceives in an erect posture must be men. Robertson calls it a vivid description of dawning sight, incomplete but sufficient to tell that they were men because they were walking. Bede supplies the comparison from ordinary experience, that trees standing thick together look so to men who see them from afar or by the dim light of night, and then reads it morally, that whoever is so long blinded that he cannot distinguish good from evil sees men as trees walking, because he sees the deeds of the multitude without the light of discretion. Ellicott extends the same figure forward, to the stage of spiritual growth at which truths are seen for the first time but not yet in their full proportions, and need a second touch of the divine hand.
25:
The completion of the cure is a small textual battleground. Clarke reports that the better copies read that he saw all things rather than all men, since his earlier view had been confused; Ellicott agrees on the reading and adds that the received text uses a word implying he was far-sighted as well as clear-sighted. Robertson parses the whole verse as a sequence, an effective aorist for the thorough look, a double compound for the complete restoration, and an imperfect for the seeing that then continued, and derives the adverb from words meaning afar and radiance, with a manuscript variant built instead on a word meaning plain. Gill draws one small conclusion from the second laying on of hands, that it settles what the earlier verse left vague, since the hands were evidently placed on the eyes after the spittle. Clarke turns the gradualness into an address to the reader, that however insignificant means may appear they are divinely efficacious when Christ chooses to work by them, and that a measure of light is ground for praying that he may lay his hands again.

The closing prohibition is explained four ways and rejected once. Barnes takes it as prudence, lest the jealousy of the Pharisees be excited and commotion follow. Clarke reads it geographically, since the man was sent home and told not to enter the village, which shows he did not live there; and he notes that a miracle recorded by no other evangelist is one more proof that Mark did not abridge the first Gospel. Ellicott reads it as spiritual discipline prescribed after the cure as well as before, partly because the work called for prayer over the right use of a restored power and partly because Christ would not seem to court publicity, and he draws the application that a first clear apprehension of spiritual truth is not well followed by the hasty utterances of a new-born excitement. Calvin reports the conjecture that the town was being punished and declines to rest on it, holding instead what he thinks certain: no miracle was performed in order to remain perpetually buried, and this one was to be concealed along with many others only until, having expiated by his death the sins of the world, he should ascend to the glory of the Father.
27:
The place is chosen as carefully as the question. Bede identifies the town and its renaming in honour of the emperor by the Philip who was Herod's brother. Robertson explains why it mattered: the district lies on a spur of Mount Hermon in territory ruled by that Philip, so that Jesus was safe here from Herod Antipas and from the Pharisees and Sadducees, and would have his best opportunity to teach the disciples about the crucifixion a little over six months ahead. Theophylact gives the same reason in his own terms, that having taken them far from the Jews he asks about himself so that they might speak the truth without fear. Bede also explains the order of the two questions, that he asks the opinion of men first in order to try the faith of the disciples, lest their confession should appear to be founded on common opinion; Chrysostom says the manner of the question was itself designed to lead them to higher thoughts, that they might not agree with the multitude. Henry draws the human lesson, that although it is a small thing to be judged of men it may sometimes do us good to know what is said of us, not that we may seek our own glory but that we may hear our faults.

Cyril of Jerusalem gives the fullest account of why the question was put at all, and it is not vanity. Our Lord had lately become Man and was by the many unknown, and wishing to teach what was not known he called his disciples and asked them, not from vain-glory but to show them the truth, lest, dwelling with the Only-begotten of God, they should think lightly of him as of some mere man. When they reported that others named a prophet, he answered that such men might be excused their ignorance, but that Apostles who in his name cleansed lepers and cast out devils ought not to be ignorant of him through whom they did those works. And when all fell silent, the matter being too high for man to learn, Peter answered, neither aided by cunning invention nor persuaded by human reasoning but enlightened in his mind from the Father. Robertson puts the same test in historical terms: the disciples had confessed him as Messiah before, but Jesus had ceased to use the word to avoid political complications, and the question is whether they still believed it after all the defections and oppositions they had seen.
29:
That Mark records the confession and omits the blessing on Peter is noticed by four witnesses, and three of them give the same reason. Theophylact says the evangelist passes over what the Lord answered and how he blessed him, lest by relating it he should seem to be favouring his own master Peter, while the other Gospel goes through the whole of it. Ellicott, assuming the same connection between the writer and the Apostle, regards the omission as evidence of Peter's humility, since he shrank from what might seem to savour of self-assertion. Robertson says plainly that Mark omits all praise of Peter, probably because Peter himself had done so in telling the story, and notes in passing the modern criticism that treats the fuller narrative as a later development meant to justify ecclesiastical prerogatives. Origen observes only the fact, that the two shorter Gospels give the confession without the additional words and therefore without the blessing that answered them. Gill lists exactly what is missing — the rock, the gates of hell, the keys, the binding and loosing — and Clarke notes that a few manuscripts supply the longer form of the confession here.

Why silence was then imposed is answered by purpose rather than prudence alone. Wesley gives three reasons at once: that he might not encourage the people to set him up for a temporal king, that he might not provoke the scribes and Pharisees to destroy him before the time, and that he might not forestall the bright evidence to be given of his divine character after the resurrection. Robertson says simply that the time was not yet ripe, and that when it came, at the entry into Jerusalem, the very stones would cry out if men did not. Chrysostom looks past the silence to what ends it, that Christ would wait to fix the pure faith in their minds until the Crucifixion, which was an offence to them, was over, and that after it was perfected he sent them to teach all nations — the point of telling them being to show that Christ must be preached by his witnesses after the cross and resurrection. Henry adds why the crowd had not reached the confession themselves, that they would have acknowledged him had their teachers not possessed them with the notion that the Messiah must be a temporal Prince appearing in outward pomp.
31:
Why the teaching begins now is answered from the confession that precedes it. Gill says that until this point he had said nothing of his sufferings in express terms, but that now, they being firmly established in the faith of him as the Messiah, he thought it proper to inform them. Robertson says the same and adds that the other Gospel dates it expressly from that time, so that the confession of faith indicated it was a good moment to begin; he notes that the death is to come at the hands of the council in which the two parties had about equal strength, and remarks that although the resurrection on the third day is mentioned it made no impression on their minds, this rainbow on the cloud not being seen. Theophylact orders the two events the same way, that only after the Lord had accepted the confession of disciples who called him true God did he reveal to them the mystery of the Cross.

The phrase about three days is disputed, and Robertson takes the dispute on. Some, he says, stickle for a strict reading of after three days which would put the rising on the fourth day rather than the third; he answers that Mark's phrase must have the same sense as the third day in the other two Gospels, or else the accounts are hopelessly contradictory, and that in popular language after three days can and often does mean on the third day, while the fourth day is impossible. On the manner of the telling every witness agrees and each adds a word: Gill says it was spoken before them all and in plain words without a figure, and spoken freely and boldly with an undaunted courage; Barnes says it was without parables so that there could be no possibility of misunderstanding; Clarke notes that the disciples now began fully to understand him and that the observation is Mark's own addition; Robertson says he held back nothing and told it all without reserve, the tense showing he did it repeatedly; Wesley adds that till now he had only intimated it.
33:
How far Peter is to be blamed divides the witnesses by degrees. Bede excuses him furthest, saying he speaks with the feelings of a man who loves and desires, as if to say that this cannot be, and that his ears cannot receive that the Son of God is to be slain. Chrysostom explains rather than excuses, asking how one gifted with a revelation from the Father could so soon fall and become unstable, and answering that it was not wonderful, since he had learnt by revelation that Jesus was the Christ but the mystery of the cross and resurrection had not yet been revealed to him; he notes too that Peter alone, from the fervour of his disposition, had the boldness to dispute. Theophylact gives the harshest reading, that Satan alone was unwilling Christ should suffer and the race of man be saved, so that Peter, savouring the things of Satan and becoming for the moment an adversary, is called by the adversary's name. Robertson agrees it was more than mere officiousness, that Peter had not risen above the level of ordinary men and deserves the name whose role he was acting, and that the temptation offered on the mountain was here offered again; the rebuke, he says, was withering, but it was needed.

What the words of the rebuke mean is where the finest distinction is drawn. Pseudo-Chrysostom points out that Christ did not say get thee behind me to the devil when he was tempted, but says it to Peter, and takes the difference to be the whole point: to Peter it means follow me, and resist not the design of my voluntary Passion. Cyril of Jerusalem reads the same exchange as proof of willingness, that others who do not foreknow their death die unwillingly while he spoke of his passion beforehand, and that he shunned death lest the whole world perish in its sins; and he closes a long list of the sins for which Christ was not crucified with this very verse, that he came to his passion not unwillingly but willing, so that if any should even now dissuade him he would answer as he answered here. Robertson supplies the staging that makes the rebuke public: Peter had drawn Jesus aside privately, but Jesus wheeled round on him and in doing so brought the other disciples into plain view, a touch only in Mark, so that the rebuke fell in the full presence of the group — and he suspects the others may have shared Peter's mind and been watching the effect. Wesley reads the same look the same way, that they might the more observe what was said.
34:
The setting is Mark's own. Robertson notes that Mark alone records the unexpected presence of a crowd up here near Caesarea Philippi in heathen territory, and that in the presence of this crowd Jesus explains his philosophy of life and death in direct contrast with the one Peter had just offered and evidently shared with the disciples and the people. Gill supplies how they came to be there: they had followed him out of Galilee and from Bethsaida, for it was on the way to Caesarea Philippi that this conversation fell, and while he and the disciples walked together alone the multitude followed at some distance, so that when the private conversation ended he beckoned to them to come nearer. Wesley reads the summons as a measure of the weight of what follows — he called the people to hear a truth of the last importance, and one that equally concerned them all.

Chrysostom fastens on the conditional form of the call and will not let it be read as compulsion. I call you to those good things which a man should wish for, he has the Lord say, I do not force you to evil and burdensome things; for he who does violence to his hearer often stands in his way, but he who leaves him free rather draws him to himself. Clarke frames the whole verse the same way and for a different reason: he thinks the conditions Christ requires are formed on those the Jews required of a proselyte, of which the first was that a man should come voluntarily and that neither force nor influence should be employed, and this Clarke takes to be the foundation of all the rest.

What self-denial amounts to is put by degrees. Chrysostom will not settle for the milder word: he says not that a man should not spare himself, but what is more, that he should deny himself, as if he had nothing in common with himself, facing danger and looking on such things as if another were suffering — and this, he insists, is really to spare himself, as parents most truly act kindly to their children when they give them up to masters with an injunction not to spare them. Theophylact presses the family image the other way: a man who denies another, be it brother or father, does not sympathize with him nor grieve at his fate though he be wounded and die, and so we ought to despise our body. Bede sets it in time rather than in feeling — we deny ourselves when we avoid what we were of old and strive to reach that point whither we are newly called. Wesley makes it a matter of will, in all things small and great, however pleasing, and that continually.

The cross divides the readings by season. Chrysostom takes it at full strength, as meaning even to the most shameful death, and adds the warning that a man may suffer and yet not follow Christ, namely when he does not suffer for Christ's sake; Theophylact explains the shame historically, that at that time the cross appeared shameful because malefactors were fixed to it. Bede allows a second sense for times without persecution: in persecution life is to be laid aside, but in peace our earthly desires are to be broken, and the cross is taken up when either our body is pained by abstinence or our soul afflicted by fellow-feeling for our neighbour. Clarke's remaining conditions run parallel, renunciation answering to a new birth, the yoke of the law answering to Christ's own doctrine and cross, and perseverance to death comprised in the last word, follow me. Pseudo-Jerome gives the reason for saying any of it so early: as a skilful pilot foreseeing a storm in a calm wishes his sailors to be prepared.
35:
Mark's wording is fuller than the parallel, and both Ellicott and Robertson stop on the surplus. Robertson observes that the phrase for the gospel's sake stands in Mark alone; Ellicott, noting that the other evangelist has simply for my sake, calls the addition significant as showing that though our Lord demanded in the first instance entire personal devotion, it was for himself as identified with the cause of the good news from God of which he had borne witness and of which he was to be the martyr. Robertson adds that two senses of the word life and two of the word save are at work in the saying, and that where Mark's final verb is save the other Gospel has find.

Which life is meant is settled briefly by Remigius, who says that life is to be taken in this place for the present life and not for the substance itself of the soul. Gill grants the instinct its due before he takes it away: life is a valuable thing and all that a man has he will give for it, self preservation is a principle in nature, and it becomes every man to take all lawful methods to save his life when it is threatened or is in danger. The loss he is describing is therefore a particular one — the man who, when his life is called for to be laid down for Christ's sake, will rather deny Christ and give up a profession of him and his Gospel than lay it down.

Chrysostom reads the command as mercy rather than severity, and says so in the same breath as the paradox: I give you these commands, as it were to spare you, for whosoever spares his son brings him to destruction, but whosoever does not spare him saves him. He then argues the point from ordinary courage. It is right to be always prepared for death, since if in the battles of this world he who is prepared for death fights better than others, though none can restore him to life after death, much more is this the case in spiritual battle, where so great a hope of resurrection is set before him, and where he who gives up his soul unto death saves it.

The question about profit is added, Chrysostom says, precisely so that nobody should suppose the loss to be equivalent to the salvation. Think not that he has saved his soul who has shunned the perils of the cross; for when a man at the cost of his soul gains the whole world, what has he besides, now that his soul is perishing? Has he another soul to give for his soul? A man can give the price of his house in exchange for the house, but in losing his soul he has not another soul to give — and the word exchange is chosen on purpose, since God in exchange for our salvation has given the precious blood of Jesus Christ. Gill argues the same arithmetic from the other end: all the riches of the world and the whole world itself are not an equivalent to the soul nor a sufficient ransom for it, riches will not profit in the day of wrath, and a man who had the whole world could not redeem his soul with it and has nothing else to give. Henry states the balance plainly, that as the happiness of heaven with Christ is enough to make up for the loss of life itself for him, so the gain of all the world in sin will not make up for the ruin of the soul by sin.
38:
What exactly is to be ashamed of is spelled out before the warning is. Gill takes the object of the shame from what has just been said — Christ as suffering, crucified and put to death — and describes the man who through scandal of the cross and fear of men dare not profess faith in him but conceals it and keeps it to himself. Barnes reads the same reluctance as embarrassment at a lowly appearance, and at poverty, contempt and sufferings; and my words, he adds, means the doctrines and the instructions. Wesley makes the confession wider than speech, as avowing whatever Christ has said, and particularly what he has said of self denial and the daily cross, both by word and by action.

Clarke traces the reluctance to a disappointed expectation, and thinks our Lord hints here at one of the principal reasons of the incredulity of the Jews: they saw nothing in the person of Jesus Christ which corresponded to the pompous notions they had formed of the Messiah, and had he come into the world as a mighty and opulent man clothed with earthly glories and honours he would have had a multitude of partisans, most of them hypocrites. The words gave a second offence on their own account, since the doctrine of the cross must be believed, a suffering Messiah acknowledged, poverty and affliction borne, and death perhaps suffered in consequence of becoming his disciples; of him and of his words in this sense, Clarke says, the world is to this day ashamed. The reciprocity he states without softening: as he refused to acknowledge me before men, so will I refuse to acknowledge him before God and his angels — and he asks who can help the man whom the only Saviour eternally disowns.

Two of the witnesses narrow the aim of the sentence. Ellicott observes that these words are absent from the first Gospel and present, though not quite verbally, in the third, and that general as they are they had a special bearing on those who, like Peter and probably the other disciples, had just shown that they were ashamed of what had been said. Robertson narrows it further, by the grammar: the verb is not a statement about the future conduct of a man but about his present attitude toward Jesus, so that the conduct of men toward Christ now determines Christ's conduct then. Barnes states the same conclusion as a series of reversals — they that would not acknowledge him here must be rejected by him there, they that would not serve him always will never enjoy him, they that would cast him out and despise him must be cast out by him.

The description of the generation is glossed two ways. Barnes takes it plainly, as an age given to wickedness and particularly to adultery, and notes that Robertson finds the phrase in this Gospel alone. Ellicott finds the force of it rather in a contrast, between those from whose frown or scorn the disciples were now shrinking and the bright hosts in whose presence the faithless should be put to shame when the Son of Man should come in his glory; they were to look on this picture and on that, and ask themselves which ordeal was the most terrible. Barnes draws the two appearances the same way, that he was lowly, meek and despised, and yet there was an inimitable beauty in his character even then, but that he will come again in awful grandeur, not as the babe of Bethlehem nor as the Man of Nazareth, but as the Son of God, in majesty and glory. Robertson adds a note on the text rather than the theme, that this saying and the one the chapter division puts after it form a single paragraph and should be read together.
